To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the log-linear models for SUBGs provide a general and powerful statistical framework for stochastic grammars, and that the two estimation techniques that we propose are both computationally tractable and yield good results in practice.

(1) the log-linear model is a good model for the stochastic SUBG; (2) the log-linear estimator is a good estimator for the parameters of this stochastic model; and (3) the stochastic SUBG provides an accurate model for a wide range of phenomena.

(i) log-linear models provide a natural framework for stochastic SUBGs and other stochastic grammars; (ii) there are two tractable ways of estimating such grammars from corpora; (iii) these estimators are not identical to each other or to the Maximum-Likelihood (ML) estimator; (iv) these estimators perform well in practice, as shown by experiments on the Penn Treebank and the Wall Street Journal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a statistical approach to the analysis of natural language syntax, based on a formalism which is both powerful and well-motivated.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a framework for stochastic "unification-based" grammars that is statistically sound and computationally efficient.
log-linear models provide a very flexible framework for modeling the stochastic behavior of grammars and can be used to model a wide variety of grammatical phenomena.
we show how to use a large amount of linguistic data to build a grammar that is more linguistically accurate and more statistically sound than previous stochastic grammars.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the estimation methods we propose can be applied to any grammar formalism that can be represented in a "unification-based" framework.
